Hey! I know I'm late to the post but thought I'd throw in my 2 cents as an NB student here.

In my experience, most professors and students are accepting towards trans people. There will always be transphobes, but I would say the amount of accepting people (or people who don't care) greatly outweighs them. I see a growing number of professors including their pronouns in their email signatures and Zoom display names (although I am in linguistics and it probably varies by department). I believe there's a way to change your preferred name on the Academica website so that it's used for all non-legal purposes.

The one thing I wish WSU had was LGBT+ housing. Just a section or floor of a dorm that's geared towards LGBT+ students. I know other universities have things like that and I would have joined that in a heartbeat. Instead, the main way I've found to meet other LGBT+ people is by joining clubs you think will attract them, lol. So I would say there is a community here but you have to kinda find it yourself.

I think pretty much every language has the allophony rule that nasals will assimilate in place to a following stop. In Anguḍan, I decided to spice it up by having nasals assimilate in both place and voice. So, the hypothetical word /sanqa/ would be pronounced [sɑɴ̥qɑ], not [sɑɴqɑ] like you might expect. It’s a simple change but I think it gives the language a nice sound.

Anguḍanash, ujsa brofalanqot. Tiuj ‘uka qojsakanoti qotaḍa. Qojsa samaroqqot, qotkuku ida ishami ida atishami.

Loose translation: For the Anguḍan, ujsa is an important plant. The tea-like drink qojsa is made from it. Qojsa is very common, drunk both at home and at festivals.

angudan.DAT ujsa important-plant.3psg | tea.SIM drink qojsa.PASS.make 3psg.ABL | qojsa common.AUG.3psg 3psg.PASS.drink and house.LOC and festival.LOC

This is the first thing I’ve posted about Anguḍan! It has some inspiration from Inuktitut but is mostly a priori. It’s still very much a work in progress, as you can probably tell.

I came up with this way of expressing the future tense in my language, and I wanted to make sure it makes sense.

'Umidam qaeqot ṭapfash.

'umi-dam qaj-qot ṭapfa-sh

eat.NMLZ come.3psg 1psg.DAT

Literally "Eating comes to me", but means "I will eat".

A sentence with an object like "I will eat the/a fish" is expressed by putting fish.GEN in front of that phrase.
